title: Idempotent matrices
summary: Idempotent means A squared equals A. Every eigenvalue is 0 or 1, the matrix is diagonalizable, and the trace equals the rank. Symmetry is not part of the definition.
intuition:
Idempotent means that applying the matrix twice is the same as applying it once: $A^2=A$. Geometrically this is what a projection does, but the word idempotent does not include a right angle. An orthogonal projection is an idempotent matrix that is also symmetric. Symmetry is an extra assumption, and it is not implied by $A^2=A$. A question that says only "idempotent" has not given you $A^\top=A$.

The polynomial $x(x-1)$ annihilates $A$, because $A^2-A=0$. The minimal polynomial divides $x(x-1)$. Those two roots are distinct, so the minimal polynomial has distinct linear factors and $A$ is diagonalizable over $\mathbb{R}$. In a diagonal form every diagonal entry is $0$ or $1$. The trace is the number of $1$s on that diagonal. The rank is the same count, because a diagonal matrix of zeros and ones has rank equal to the number of ones, and rank is unchanged by invertible factors $P$ and $P^{-1}$. Therefore $\mathrm{trace}(A)=\mathrm{rank}(A)$. The eigenvalues, which are those diagonal entries, are only $0$ and $1$.

None of that argument used $A^\top=A$. The $2\times 2$ matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $A^2=A$, has trace $1$ and rank $1$, and is not symmetric. It is the example to keep against the claim that every idempotent matrix is a symmetric projection.

definitions.body: A square matrix $A$ is idempotent when $A^2=A$. Symmetry is not part of the definition. An orthogonal projection is the special case that is also symmetric.
Every eigenvalue of an idempotent matrix is $0$ or $1$. If $Av=\lambda v$ with $v\neq 0$, then $\lambda^2 v=A^2 v=Av=\lambda v$, so $\lambda^2=\lambda$.

For a real idempotent matrix, $\mathrm{trace}(A)=\mathrm{rank}(A)$. The reason is diagonalizability: the minimal polynomial divides $x(x-1)$, so $A$ is similar to a diagonal matrix of zeros and ones, and both the trace and the rank count the ones.

formulas.name: Idempotent
formulas.note: Eigenvalues are $0$ or $1$, and $\mathrm{trace}(A)=\mathrm{rank}(A)$. Symmetry is extra: it is not implied.

formulas.name: Why the trace equals the rank
formulas.note: The minimal polynomial divides $x(x-1)$. Distinct linear factors imply that $A$ is diagonalizable, with diagonal entries $0$ or $1$.

properties: $A^2=A$ forces every eigenvalue to be $0$ or $1$. No other real or complex number satisfies $\lambda^2=\lambda$ and can appear.
The minimal polynomial divides $x(x-1)$. Distinct linear factors imply that every idempotent matrix is diagonalizable over $\mathbb{R}$.
$\mathrm{trace}(A)=\mathrm{rank}(A)$. Both numbers count the eigenvalues equal to $1$.
Symmetry is not implied. There are idempotent matrices with $A^\top\neq A$.
If $A$ is idempotent then so is $I-A$, because $(I-A)^2=I-2A+A^2=I-A$. And $\mathrm{rank}(A)+\mathrm{rank}(I-A)=n$.

examples.title: A non-symmetric $2\times 2$ idempotent matrix
examples.prompt: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$. Compute $A^2$, and compare $A$ with $A^\top$, the trace, and the rank.
steps: The transpose is $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, which is not $A$ because the off-diagonal entries $1$ and $0$ disagree. Idempotence did not produce symmetry.

The trace is $1+0=1$. The second row is zero and the first row is not, so the rank is $1$. The characteristic polynomial is $(1-\lambda)(-\lambda)$, so the eigenvalues are $1$ and $0$. Trace, rank, and the number of eigenvalues equal to $1$ all agree.
examples.answer: $A^2=A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$. The matrix is not symmetric, and $\mathrm{trace}(A)=\mathrm{rank}(A)=1$.

examples.title: Another non-symmetric example, and $I-A$
examples.prompt: Let $B=\begin{pmatrix}2&-2\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$. Compute $B^2$. Then, with $A$ as in the previous example, compute $(I-A)^2$.
steps: $B^\top=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\-2&-1\end{pmatrix}\neq B$. The trace is $2+(-1)=1$. The second row is half the first, so the rank is $1$. Again the trace equals the rank, without symmetry.

For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, one has $I-A=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Then $(I-A)^2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=I-A$. The complement is idempotent and not symmetric either.
examples.answer: $B^2=B$ and $B$ is not symmetric, with trace and rank both equal to $1$. Also $(I-A)^2=I-A$.

traps: Adding symmetry to the definition. $A^2=A$ does not imply $A^\top=A$. The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ is a counterexample, and its square really is itself.

Thinking a non-symmetric idempotent matrix fails to be diagonalizable. The minimal polynomial still divides $x(x-1)$, so it is diagonalizable. Symmetry is what upgrades the diagonalization to an orthogonal one, as in the symmetric-matrix spectral theorem.
Replacing $\mathrm{trace}(A)=\mathrm{rank}(A)$ by $\mathrm{trace}(A)=n$ or by the ambient dimension. The trace counts only the eigenvalues equal to $1$.
Using the orthogonal-matrix test $A^\top A=I$ on an idempotent matrix. Unless $A=I$, an idempotent matrix has a zero eigenvalue and cannot be orthogonal.
python:
def mul(A, B):
    n = len(B)
    return [[sum(A[i][k] * B[k][j] for k in range(n)) for j in range(len(B[0]))] for i in range(len(A))]

A = [[1, 1], [0, 0]]
assert mul(A, A) == A
assert A != [list(row) for row in zip(*A)]
assert A[0][0] + A[1][1] == 1
B = [[2, -2], [1, -1]]
assert mul(B, B) == B
assert B[0][0] + B[1][1] == 1
ImA = [[0, -1], [0, 1]]
assert mul(ImA, ImA) == ImA
print(1)

questions.stem: A square matrix $A$ is idempotent when
questions.solution: The answer is **B**. Idempotent means $A^2=A$ and nothing else. Option A is the orthogonal-matrix equation. Option C is symmetry, which an orthogonal projection adds on top of idempotence and which a general idempotent matrix need not have. Option D is again the orthogonal case.

questions.stem: Every eigenvalue of a real idempotent matrix is
questions.solution: The answer is **B**. If $Av=\lambda v$ with $v\neq 0$, then $\lambda^2 v=A^2 v=Av=\lambda v$, so $\lambda(\lambda-1)=0$. The only possibilities are $0$ and $1$. Option A describes determinants of orthogonal matrices, not eigenvalues of idempotent ones. The zero eigenvalue occurs whenever $A\neq I$.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true of every real idempotent matrix $A$?
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, B, and D**. Since $A^2-A=0$, the minimal polynomial divides $x(x-1)$. The roots are distinct, so $A$ is diagonalizable, and the diagonal entries are $0$ or $1$. The trace and the rank both count the ones. Symmetry is not implied: $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ is idempotent and not symmetric.

questions.stem: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$. Which of the following are true?
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, C, and D**. The product is $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$. The trace is $1$ and the second row is zero, so the rank is $1$. The transpose is $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, which is not $A$.

The answer is **1**. The $(1,2)$ entry of the product is $(1)(1)+(1)(0)=1$. The whole product equals $A$, so this entry is also the $(1,2)$ entry of $A$. The computation is the check that $A$ is idempotent.
